## Design a Live Chat Support System

> **Core Concept:** The hard part isn't sending chat messages, it's the **routing layer** sitting in front of them: deciding which of possibly many available agents (with different skills, languages, and current loads) should get this specific incoming chat, and doing it fast enough that a visitor doesn't sit staring at 'connecting you to an agent' for a noticeable amount of time.

### Problem Statement
Design a live chat support system like Intercom: a visitor on a website
opens a chat widget and is connected to either a bot or a human support
agent. The system must route incoming chats to an available agent (or a
queue if none are free), support handoff from bot to human mid-conversation
without losing context, and let whichever agent picks up a chat see the
full history and any context gathered so far. Design the system end to end.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: Should routing be purely 'first available agent' or skill-based, matching a chat to an agent who speaks the visitor's language or handles a specific product area?
*Why it matters:* Pure round-robin to any available agent is a much simpler matching problem than skill-based routing, which needs agents tagged with capabilities and a matching/scoring step before assignment, and changes what 'available' even means (available for this specific chat, not just available in general).

#### Q: Can a chat start with a bot and hand off to a human, and if so, does the human need the full bot conversation history and any structured data the bot collected?
*Why it matters:* If handoff needs to preserve context, the conversation and any bot-collected metadata (like 'order number: 1234') must live in **one continuous record** from the start, not two disconnected systems, which affects the core data model, not just the routing logic.

#### Q: What should happen to an incoming chat when every matching agent is currently busy: queue it, offer a callback, or route to a lower-priority agent?
*Why it matters:* This decides whether the system needs a durable, ordered per-skill-group queue with wait-time estimation, which is a real subsystem, versus a simpler design that always finds someone, even at the cost of an imperfect skill match.

#### Q: How many concurrent chats can a single agent realistically handle, one at a time or several in parallel?
*Why it matters:* If agents handle multiple chats concurrently (common in real support tools), 'agent availability' becomes a capacity threshold rather than a boolean, which changes the routing algorithm from simple assignment to load-aware assignment.

### Functional Requirements
- A visitor can open a chat widget and start a conversation, which is routed to a bot, then optionally handed off to a human agent.
- The system routes an incoming chat to an available agent, considering skill/language match and current agent load, or queues it if no agent is available.
- Whichever agent (bot or human) picks up a conversation can see its full message history and any context/metadata collected so far.
- An agent can see their queue of assigned and waiting conversations and respond to messages in real time.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- Message delivery within an active chat must feel real-time, well under a second of perceived delay.
- Routing an incoming chat to an agent (or into a queue) must happen quickly, within a couple seconds, since a visitor deciding whether to wait is happening in that window.
- The system must remain available and continue routing chats even if a subset of agent-facing app servers fail, no visitor should be stuck with an unroutable chat.
- Conversation history and context must never be lost across a bot-to-human handoff or an agent-to-agent transfer.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Peak concurrent chats:** 500,000 concurrent conversations, each needing an open real-time connection (WebSocket) held by the visitor and, if assigned, the agent
- **Message throughput at peak:** 500,000 chats * (20 messages / 600 seconds) ≈ 16,700 messages/sec at peak across the platform
- **Routing decisions per second:** New chats arriving: assuming average chat duration 10 min, 500,000 concurrent / 600 sec ≈ 833 new chats/sec needing a routing decision, each of which must complete in low seconds
- **Daily message storage:** 833 new chats/sec * 86,400 sec/day * 20 messages * 500 bytes ≈ 833*86,400 ≈ 72 million chats/day * 20 * 500 bytes ≈ 720 GB/day, easily handled by a sharded store

*Summary:* The system is bottlenecked by two very different things at once: real-time message fan-out to hundreds of thousands of concurrently open connections, and a routing decision that has to run for every one of the roughly 800+ new chats arriving per second, which is why the architecture splits cleanly into a **messaging/connection layer** and a separate **routing/queueing layer** rather than one monolithic chat server.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
A router that only ever assigns a chat to an agent with a perfect skill match (right language, right product area) is simple to reason about but can leave a visitor waiting a long time if the only matching agents are all busy while less-perfectly-matched agents sit idle. The alternative is a scored match: rank available agents by how well they fit, and after a wait threshold, relax the requirement and assign to the best available agent even if imperfect.

#### undefined
Because bot and human messages live in **one shared conversation timeline** (not two separate systems bridged at handoff time), 'get context' is just 'load the conversation's message history and structured_data fields,' the same read path regardless of whether the previous turn was a bot or a person. The alternative, where bot conversations live in a separate transcript system that gets summarized and attached at handoff, avoids one shared schema but introduces a lossy translation step exactly at the moment context matters most.

lesson.content:
## Design a Live Sports Score System

> **Core Concept:** This is a **fan-out** problem in the opposite shape from a social feed: instead of many independent writers each needing to reach their own small audience, it's an extreme few-to-many broadcast, a handful of events per minute that must reach millions of identical subscribers simultaneously, so the entire design is about the delivery fan-out, not the data itself.

### Problem Statement
Design a live sports score system: as games are played, scores, game
events (goals, points, fouls), and status updates need to reach millions of
fans watching on their phones, within seconds of happening in real life.
A single popular game (a World Cup final, a playoff game) can have tens of
millions of people watching the same score update arrive at nearly the same
instant. Design the system end to end.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: How many concurrent viewers can a single popular game have, and how spiky is that number around a big moment?
*Why it matters:* A goal scored in a World Cup final might cause tens of millions of clients to need the same update within seconds, all at once. This single fact determines whether a simple pub/sub fan-out can keep up or whether a tiered broadcast/edge-caching layer is required to avoid a thundering herd on the origin.

#### Q: Do clients need push delivery (WebSocket/SSE), or is short-interval polling acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Push delivery scales the connection count problem (millions of long-lived open connections) but minimizes latency and wasted requests. Polling is operationally simpler and stateless, but either hammers the backend with redundant requests or adds unacceptable latency if the poll interval is too long, unless it's layered behind a CDN.

#### Q: How much staleness is acceptable? Does a fan need to see a goal within 1 second, or is 5-10 seconds fine?
*Why it matters:* Sub-second delivery to tens of millions of clients is a materially harder and more expensive engineering problem than a design tolerant of several seconds of lag, which opens the door to caching and batched fan-out layers that a stricter latency bar would rule out.

#### Q: Do we need to support arbitrary sports and leagues simultaneously, or can we assume traffic concentrates on one or a few marquee games at a time?
*Why it matters:* A system serving thousands of low-traffic amateur games at once is a differently-shaped load (long tail, low fan-out per game) than one where 90% of concurrent load funnels through a single marquee game (extreme fan-out on one topic), and the two call for different sharding strategies for the pub/sub layer.

### Functional Requirements
- A fan can view the live score and current status of an in-progress game.
- A fan can subscribe to a specific game and receive push updates for score changes and major events as they happen.
- The system ingests game events from an official data feed (scorers, referees, or a data provider) and reflects them in near real time.
- A fan can view a schedule of games and final scores for completed games.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- Updates for a live event must reach subscribed clients within a few seconds of the event actually happening on the field.
- The system must handle extreme simultaneous fan-out for a single popular game, tens of millions of clients needing the same update within the same short window, without falling over.
- The system must stay available and keep serving current scores even if the push delivery layer for a subset of clients degrades, falling back to a slower but working path rather than showing nothing.
- Read traffic (score checks) vastly outnumbers write traffic (actual scoring events), and the design must not let read load compete with the low-latency ingestion of new events.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Fan-out messages for one scoring event on the marquee game:** 20,000,000 subscribed clients * 1 event = 20 million push deliveries triggered by a single goal, the number that defines the whole delivery architecture
- **Sustained event rate into the system:** 20 events over 2 hours ≈ 1 event every 6 minutes for one game; even with thousands of simultaneous games, total ingestion write volume stays low (well under 100 events/sec platform-wide)
- **Push delivery bandwidth for one marquee event:** 20,000,000 deliveries * 200 bytes ≈ 4 GB of outbound data triggered in a burst of a few seconds by a single goal
- **Open connection count for the marquee game alone:** 20 million concurrent WebSocket/SSE connections just for one game, which no single server can hold, forcing horizontal sharding of the connection layer itself

*Summary:* Ingestion write volume is trivially small (under 100 events/sec platform-wide) but delivery fan-out is enormous (20 million pushes and 4 GB outbound from a single event), so the defining architectural fact is that this system is bottlenecked entirely on broadcast fan-out and connection management, not on writes, and the whole design exists to turn one rare write into millions of cheap, parallel reads.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
Push delivery means a client opens a long-lived connection and the server writes to it the instant an event happens, giving near-instant delivery but requiring the infrastructure to hold millions of concurrent open connections, which has to be sharded across many connection-holding servers, each subscribed to a pub/sub topic per game so it knows what to push to its slice of clients. Polling means the client repeatedly asks 'what's the score now,' which is trivially stateless and cacheable behind a CDN, but either the poll interval is short enough to feel real-time (and multiplies read load enormously) or it's long enough to be cheap (and feels laggy).

#### undefined
Publishing one event and having a single process try to push it to 20 million sockets is not viable on any single machine. The connection-holding tier is sharded across many servers, each holding some slice of the total connections for a given game (say, 50,000-100,000 connections per node). A pub/sub backbone (e.g. Redis pub/sub, Kafka, or a dedicated broadcast service) delivers the single published event to every connection-holding node subscribed to that game's topic, and each node then fans it out only to its own local slice of sockets in parallel.

lesson.content:
## Design a Live Streaming Platform (Twitch)

> **Core Concept:** Every viewer is watching the same seconds of video at the same moment, which means fan-out here is 'one stream to millions of concurrent viewers,' the mirror image of Twitter's 'one post to millions of followers over time,' and the whole system has to trade **latency for scale** on a moving deadline that never gets to relax, because there is no finished file to cache, only the last few seconds that matter.

### Problem Statement
Design a live streaming platform like Twitch: a broadcaster pushes a live
video feed from their own encoder, and potentially millions of viewers
watch that same feed simultaneously with only a few seconds of delay,
while also participating in a live text chat alongside the stream. Design
the system end to end, from ingest to viewer playback and chat.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: How much end-to-end latency is acceptable between the broadcaster's camera and a viewer's screen?
*Why it matters:* Sub-second latency (for real interactivity) needs a fundamentally different, much more expensive protocol stack (like WebRTC) than 'a few seconds is fine' (which allows chunked HLS/DASH-style delivery through a CDN, dramatically cheaper at scale). This single answer decides almost the entire ingest and delivery architecture.

#### Q: Do all viewers of a given stream need to be in sync with each other (e.g. for shared live reactions), or is a few seconds of per-viewer drift acceptable?
*Why it matters:* CDN edge caching, the only realistic way to serve millions of concurrent viewers, inherently introduces small per-viewer timing differences. Requiring perfect viewer-to-viewer sync would rule out CDN-based delivery entirely and force a much more expensive direct-fan-out architecture.

#### Q: What's the expected distribution of concurrent viewers per stream: mostly small streams, or do a few channels regularly hit hundreds of thousands of simultaneous viewers?
*Why it matters:* A small-streams-only platform could almost get away with simpler direct delivery. A platform with viral, six-figure-concurrent-viewer channels absolutely requires CDN fan-out and multi-bitrate adaptive delivery, since no single origin server can push that much simultaneous bandwidth.

#### Q: Does live chat need message history and moderation tooling, or just best-effort real-time delivery while the stream is live?
*Why it matters:* Chat as a throwaway, high-volume real-time firehose (no durability requirement) is a much simpler pub/sub problem than chat with persistence, replay, and moderation, which starts to need its own storage and indexing layer.

### Functional Requirements
- A broadcaster can start a live stream from an encoder (e.g. OBS) and have it become watchable by viewers within a few seconds.
- A viewer can watch any live stream, with the player adapting stream quality to their network conditions.
- Viewers can post and see live chat messages alongside the stream in near real time.
- The stream ends and, optionally, is saved as an on-demand video-on-demand (VOD) replay.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- Glass-to-glass latency (camera to viewer screen) should be low, on the order of a few seconds, not tens of seconds, or the product stops feeling live.
- The system must support fan-out of a single stream to hundreds of thousands or millions of concurrent viewers without the broadcaster's origin connection being the bottleneck.
- High availability for playback: a popular stream going down mid-broadcast affects a huge simultaneous audience at once, so the delivery path needs redundancy the ingest path can tolerate being simpler about.
- Chat must handle extremely high message throughput on popular channels (thousands of messages per second) without messages arriving so far out of order or so delayed that the conversation becomes incoherent.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Total concurrent viewers:** (50,000 channels - 100 top channels) * 200 avg + 100 top channels * 50,000 = 49,900 * 200 + 100 * 50,000 ≈ 9.98M + 5M ≈ 15 million concurrent viewers platform-wide
- **Ingest bandwidth:** 50,000 concurrent streams * 6 Mbps ≈ 300 Gbps of raw ingest bandwidth arriving continuously, which must land on a distributed set of ingest points, not one datacenter
- **Transcoding compute:** 50,000 concurrent streams * 4 renditions, each needing real-time (1x) encode speed since this is live, not batch: 200,000 concurrent real-time encode jobs, which must run on a large, elastic, low-latency-optimized worker fleet, very different from YouTube's batch transcoding farm
- **Peak egress bandwidth:** 15,000,000 concurrent viewers * ~3 Mbps average delivered bitrate across the rendition mix / 8 bits ≈ roughly 5.6 Tbps sustained egress, which must be absorbed almost entirely by CDN edge capacity, not origin

*Summary:* The single fact that drives this whole architecture is that a stream has no finished file to fall back on: viewers are all converging on the last few seconds of an ever-growing, never-complete asset, so caching has to work on a **rolling window** of fresh segments (unlike YouTube's cache-forever finished files), and both transcoding and delivery must sustain real-time throughput continuously, with ==zero tolerance for backlog== that on-demand video could absorb.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
A feed's fan-out problem is 'one post reaches many followers, spread out over however long they each next open the app,' which is why caching a pre-computed per-user timeline works. A live stream's fan-out problem is 'the same few seconds of video must reach every current viewer at nearly the same instant,' which is exactly the shape a CDN's shared edge cache is built for: the first viewer's request in a region pulls a segment from origin, every other simultaneous viewer in that region is served the identical cached segment, so the cost of the 50,001st viewer of the same segment is nearly zero.

#### undefined
Chunked HTTP delivery (segmenting video into small files, e.g. 2-6 seconds each, distributed like any other CDN-cacheable object) is what makes CDN caching possible at all, but each chunk boundary adds latency, typically totaling several seconds end to end. A persistent low-latency protocol like WebRTC can get glass-to-glass latency under a second, but it's a stateful, per-viewer connection that a traditional CDN can't cache or fan out the same way, so it scales far worse for very large simultaneous audiences.

*Why it matters:* Sub-second latency (for real interactivity) needs a fundamentally different, much more expensive protocol stack (like WebRTC) than 'a few seconds is fine' (which allows chunked HLS/DASH-style delivery through a CDN, dramatically cheaper at scale). This single answer decides almost the entire ingest and delivery architecture.

#### Q: Do all viewers of a given stream need to be in sync with each other (e.g. for shared live reactions), or is a few seconds of per-viewer drift acceptable?
*Why it matters:* CDN edge caching, the only realistic way to serve millions of concurrent viewers, inherently introduces small per-viewer timing differences. Requiring perfect viewer-to-viewer sync would rule out CDN-based delivery entirely and force a much more expensive direct-fan-out architecture.

#### Q: What's the expected distribution of concurrent viewers per stream: mostly small streams, or do a few channels regularly hit hundreds of thousands of simultaneous viewers?
*Why it matters:* A small-streams-only platform could almost get away with simpler direct delivery. A platform with viral, six-figure-concurrent-viewer channels absolutely requires CDN fan-out and multi-bitrate adaptive delivery, since no single origin server can push that much simultaneous bandwidth.

#### Q: Does live chat need message history and moderation tooling, or just best-effort real-time delivery while the stream is live?
*Why it matters:* Chat as a throwaway, high-volume real-time firehose (no durability requirement) is a much simpler pub/sub problem than chat with persistence, replay, and moderation, which starts to need its own storage and indexing layer.

### Functional Requirements
- A broadcaster can start a live stream from an encoder (e.g. OBS) and have it become watchable by viewers within a few seconds.
- A viewer can watch any live stream, with the player adapting stream quality to their network conditions.
- Viewers can post and see live chat messages alongside the stream in near real time.
- The stream ends and, optionally, is saved as an on-demand video-on-demand (VOD) replay.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- Glass-to-glass latency (camera to viewer screen) should be low, on the order of a few seconds, not tens of seconds, or the product stops feeling live.
- The system must support fan-out of a single stream to hundreds of thousands or millions of concurrent viewers without the broadcaster's origin connection being the bottleneck.
- High availability for playback: a popular stream going down mid-broadcast affects a huge simultaneous audience at once, so the delivery path needs redundancy the ingest path can tolerate being simpler about.
- Chat must handle extremely high message throughput on popular channels (thousands of messages per second) without messages arriving so far out of order or so delayed that the conversation becomes incoherent.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Total concurrent viewers:** (50,000 channels - 100 top channels) * 200 avg + 100 top channels * 50,000 = 49,900 * 200 + 100 * 50,000 ≈ 9.98M + 5M ≈ 15 million concurrent viewers platform-wide
- **Ingest bandwidth:** 50,000 concurrent streams * 6 Mbps ≈ 300 Gbps of raw ingest bandwidth arriving continuously, which must land on a distributed set of ingest points, not one datacenter
- **Transcoding compute:** 50,000 concurrent streams * 4 renditions, each needing real-time (1x) encode speed since this is live, not batch: 200,000 concurrent real-time encode jobs, which must run on a large, elastic, low-latency-optimized worker fleet, very different from YouTube's batch transcoding farm
- **Peak egress bandwidth:** 15,000,000 concurrent viewers * ~3 Mbps average delivered bitrate across the rendition mix / 8 bits ≈ roughly 5.6 Tbps sustained egress, which must be absorbed almost entirely by CDN edge capacity, not origin

*Summary:* The single fact that drives this whole architecture is that a stream has no finished file to fall back on: viewers are all converging on the last few seconds of an ever-growing, never-complete asset, so caching has to work on a **rolling window** of fresh segments (unlike YouTube's cache-forever finished files), and both transcoding and delivery must sustain real-time throughput continuously, with ==zero tolerance for backlog== that on-demand video could absorb.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
A feed's fan-out problem is 'one post reaches many followers, spread out over however long they each next open the app,' which is why caching a pre-computed per-user timeline works. A live stream's fan-out problem is 'the same few seconds of video must reach every current viewer at nearly the same instant,' which is exactly the shape a CDN's shared edge cache is built for: the first viewer's request in a region pulls a segment from origin, every other simultaneous viewer in that region is served the identical cached segment, so the cost of the 50,001st viewer of the same segment is nearly zero.

#### undefined
Chunked HTTP delivery (segmenting video into small files, e.g. 2-6 seconds each, distributed like any other CDN-cacheable object) is what makes CDN caching possible at all, but each chunk boundary adds latency, typically totaling several seconds end to end. A persistent low-latency protocol like WebRTC can get glass-to-glass latency under a second, but it's a stateful, per-viewer connection that a traditional CDN can't cache or fan out the same way, so it scales far worse for very large simultaneous audiences.

callout.text: Every viewer is watching the same seconds of video at the same moment, which means fan-out here is 'one stream to millions of concurrent viewers,' the mirror image of Twitter's 'one post to millions of followers over time,' and the whole system has to trade **latency for scale** on a moving deadline that never gets to relax, because there is no finished file to cache, only the last few seconds that matter.

## Design a Log Search / Analytics System (Splunk-style)

> **Core Concept:** The ingestion rate is so far beyond what can be fully indexed forever that **retention** itself becomes a design dimension, not an afterthought: the system has to decide, continuously, which data deserves expensive full indexing right now versus which data ages into a cheaper, coarser form, and ==that decision shapes every other component==.

### Problem Statement
Design a log search and analytics system: many services across a large
organization continuously emit log lines, and users need to run full-text
and structured (field-based) queries over recent and historical logs,
see results within seconds, and build dashboards and alerts on top of
them. Design the ingestion, indexing, and query system end to end.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: What's the total log ingestion volume, and how bursty is it (e.g. does an incident cause a 10x spike in log volume)?
*Why it matters:* Ingestion rate determines whether a write path needs to be a simple queue-and-index pipeline or a heavily buffered, backpressure-aware system, and incident-time bursts (exactly when logs matter most) are often the worst-case load the system must survive.

#### Q: How long does data need to stay fully, fast-searchable, versus how long does it need to be retained at all (even if slower or summarized)?
*Why it matters:* A 'search anything, instantly, forever' requirement is enormously more expensive than 'fast search on the last 7 days, slower search or rollups beyond that.' This directly decides the storage tiering strategy and overall cost.

#### Q: Do queries need full-text search (free-text terms across unstructured messages) or structured field queries (field=value, numeric ranges), or both simultaneously?
*Why it matters:* Full-text search needs an inverted index; structured field queries are often served better by columnar or field-value indexes. Needing both well means maintaining two complementary index structures over the same data, not just one.

#### Q: Do users need real-time alerting on incoming logs (e.g. 'notify me within a minute if error rate spikes'), or is query-time analysis on already-ingested data enough?
*Why it matters:* Real-time alerting requires a streaming evaluation path running alongside ingestion, separate from the indexed-search path, since waiting for data to be fully indexed and queryable would make alerts too slow to be useful.

### Functional Requirements
- Services can continuously send log lines (structured or unstructured) to the system for ingestion.
- Users can run full-text search queries over log message content and get matching lines back, ranked or ordered by time.
- Users can run structured queries filtering on specific fields (service=checkout, status_code>=500) combined with time ranges.
- Older log data ages out of full indexing according to a retention policy, while remaining available in a cheaper, coarser form for a longer period.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- Ingestion must sustain very high, bursty write throughput without dropping logs, especially during incidents when log volume spikes and matters most.
- Search queries over recent (hot) data should return in a small number of seconds, since this system is frequently used for live incident debugging.
- The system must scale storage costs sublinearly with total retained history, by rolling up or compressing older data rather than keeping everything fully indexed forever.
- The system must tolerate ingestion or indexing slowdowns gracefully (queue and catch up) rather than losing log data outright.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Log lines ingested per day:** 500,000,000,000,000 bytes / 300 bytes per line ≈ 1.67 trillion log lines/day across the organization
- **Average and peak ingestion rate:** 1.67 trillion lines / 86,400 sec ≈ 19.3 million lines/sec average; incident-time bursts commonly hit 3x that, so design ingestion for roughly 55-60 million lines/sec at peak
- **Hot tier storage footprint:** 500 TB/day raw * 7 days = 3.5 PB of raw log data held in the hot tier at any time; with ~125% index overhead, the indexed hot tier footprint is roughly 3.5 PB * 2.25 ≈ 7.9 PB
- **Cold tier storage footprint:** 500 TB/day raw * 358 remaining days ≈ 179 PB of raw data over a year, but rolled-up/compressed cold storage (aggregates plus compressed raw, not a full secondary index) shrinks this dramatically, commonly to a fraction of the hot tier's per-byte cost

*Summary:* The single driving fact is that daily ingestion (tens of millions of lines/sec, hundreds of terabytes/day) makes keeping everything fully indexed forever both prohibitively expensive and unnecessary for how the data is actually used, so the system is built around a hot/cold, fully-indexed/rolled-up tiering strategy from the start, not bolted on later as a cost optimization.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
Free-text search (find log lines containing 'connection refused') is naturally served by an inverted index, term to matching document IDs, the same structure a search engine uses. Structured queries (status_code >= 500 AND service = checkout) are naturally served by a columnar or field-value index, which stores each field's values contiguously so range and equality filters can skip most of the data. Building both structures over the same ingested data, rather than trying to force one structure to serve both query types well, is what keeps each query type fast.

#### undefined
Keeping every log line fully indexed for a year would mean the indexed footprint keeps growing at the full ingestion rate indefinitely, which is both extremely expensive and mostly wasted, since the overwhelming majority of queries target recent data. A tiered retention model keeps a short, fully-indexed hot window for fast interactive search, then rolls older data into two cheaper forms: compressed raw blobs (for the rare case someone needs the exact original lines) and precomputed rollup aggregates (counts, error rates, per-service volume by hour) that answer the majority of historical questions without ever touching raw data again.

lesson.content:
## Design a Music Recommendation System

> **Core Concept:** The recommendation model doesn't need to run per request at all, taste barely shifts minute to minute, so the entire design problem is splitting the work into a heavy **offline batch pipeline** that computes recommendations ahead of time and a featherweight **online path** that just serves what's already been computed, and ==cold start== is what breaks that split for anyone without history yet.

### Problem Statement
Design a music recommendation system like Spotify's Discover Weekly: a
personalized playlist of tracks a user has probably never heard but is
likely to enjoy, generated from their listening history, refreshed on a
regular cadence, and served instantly whenever they open it. Design the
system end to end, including how it handles a brand-new user or a
brand-new track with no listening history at all.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: Do recommendations need to update within the same session, for example right after a user skips several songs, or is a daily or weekly refresh acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Session-level responsiveness needs an online re-ranking layer on top of whatever is precomputed. A weekly cadence, like Discover Weekly itself, lets nearly the whole system be offline batch, a much simpler design.

#### Q: What data do we have to work with, just listening history and skips, or also the audio content itself, genre, tempo, acoustic features?
*Why it matters:* This decides whether collaborative filtering alone is viable or whether content-based signals are required, especially for new or unpopular tracks with little listening history to learn from.

#### Q: How should we handle brand-new users with no listening history, and brand-new or niche tracks with almost no plays?
*Why it matters:* Cold start on both sides needs a fundamentally different strategy, content-based or popularity-based, than the collaborative filtering that works fine once a user or track has enough history.

#### Q: What serving latency is acceptable, and does the recommendation list need to be computed at request time or can it be precomputed?
*Why it matters:* Precomputing recommendations offline turns the online path into a simple key lookup, dramatically simplifying the latency story versus scoring millions of tracks live on every request.

### Functional Requirements
- A user is served a personalized playlist of recommended tracks, refreshed on a regular cadence.
- The system learns from a user's listening behavior, plays, skips, likes, repeats, to improve future recommendations.
- A new user with little or no listening history still receives a reasonable set of recommendations.
- A new or niche track with little play history can still be recommended based on its own content characteristics, not just popularity.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- Serving recommendations must be low latency, well under a second, since it's a page a user opens often.
- The system must scale to hundreds of millions of users against tens of millions of tracks without training or serving cost growing unmanageably with catalog size.
- Recommendation quality must degrade gracefully for cold-start users and tracks rather than returning nothing at all.
- The offline training pipeline's compute cost and duration must never block or degrade the online serving path; training can be slow, serving cannot.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Daily interaction events logged:** 600,000,000 users times 50 events/day is 30,000,000,000 events/day, the input volume for the offline training pipeline and any near-real-time session signals
- **Size of the user-track interaction matrix:** 600,000,000 users times 100,000,000 tracks is 6 times 10 to the 16th possible cells; even at a generous 0.001 percent actual density, that is still roughly 600 million recorded interactions, which is why this has to be stored and processed as a sparse matrix, a dense representation is computationally impossible at this scale
- **Weekly batch recommendation compute:** 600 million users times a candidate set of a few thousand tracks scored per user for the weekly playlist is on the order of trillions of score computations per week, only feasible as a scheduled offline batch job spread across a cluster over hours, not a per-request online computation
- **Precomputed recommendation storage:** 600,000,000 users times 30 recommended track IDs times about 8 bytes/ID is roughly 144 GB to store every user's precomputed weekly playlist, small enough to sit entirely in a distributed key-value store for instant lookup at serve time

*Summary:* The driving fact is that the interaction matrix is enormous, 6 times 10 to the 16th cells, but ==extremely sparse==, so the expensive part, **matrix factorization** over that sparsity, is only tractable as a scheduled offline batch job, which is exactly why the online serving path reduces to a roughly 144 GB key-value lookup of already-computed results instead of live model inference.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
Collaborative filtering infers taste from patterns across many users, users who listened to X also listened to Y, needing no understanding of the audio itself, and it improves as interaction data grows. Content-based filtering instead recommends based on a track's own characteristics, genre, tempo, acoustic embedding, matched to what a user has liked, needing no other users' data on that track at all.

#### undefined
Matrix factorization over billions of interactions is expensive and slow, running it per request would blow any reasonable latency budget for a result that barely changes minute to minute for most users. Splitting into a slow offline training path and a fast online serving path removes that pressure entirely.

#### undefined
A new user has no taste vector to build on since collaborative filtering requires prior interactions, and a new track has no play data to correlate with other tracks. Both need a bootstrap path that doesn't depend on the signal neither of them has yet.

lesson.content:
## Design a Nearby Search Service (Yelp)

> **Core Concept:** The hard part isn't choosing a single clever geospatial data structure, it's that 'nearby' and 'matches ramen' are answered by two completely different kinds of index, a **spatial structure** and a **text/inverted index**, and naively running one filter then the other throws away most of the other index's power, so the real design question is how to combine them into one fast query.

### Problem Statement
Design a service like Yelp: users can search for businesses matching a
text query (e.g. "ramen") within a given distance of their current
location, and results come back ranked by a mix of relevance and
distance. Businesses have relatively static profiles (name, category,
address, rating) that are updated far less often than they're searched.
Design the system end to end.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: Is the search always 'text query plus a distance radius,' or does it also need to support pure category browsing with no text (e.g. 'show me all coffee shops nearby')?
*Why it matters:* Pure category/location browsing with no free text is a much simpler query, essentially just the spatial filter. If free-text relevance search is a first-class, always-present part of the query, the design has to seriously address combining a spatial index with a text index, not just bolt text search on as an afterthought.

#### Q: How static are business locations and profiles, do they change roughly daily (new photos, hours) or almost never (address, category)?
*Why it matters:* This is a read-heavy system regardless, but the update cadence determines whether the combined spatial-plus-text index can be rebuilt in large batches on a comfortable schedule, or needs a more real-time incremental update path. Low write volume means the design can lean toward index structures that are cheap to query but relatively expensive to update, since updates are rare.

#### Q: Does ranking need to account for more than distance and text relevance, like star rating, review count, or sponsored placement?
*Why it matters:* Pure distance-plus-relevance ranking is a two-factor scoring function. Adding rating, popularity, or paid placement turns ranking into a genuinely multi-factor scoring problem that changes how aggressively the system can pre-filter candidates before ranking, since a business slightly farther away but much higher-rated might need to outrank a closer, mediocre one.

#### Q: What's the typical search radius and business density, a dense city block or a 20-mile suburban radius?

lesson.content:
## Design Netflix

> **Core Concept:** Because the catalog is small, fixed, and known in advance rather than a torrent of unpredictable user uploads, this system can afford to do all the expensive work (encoding every title into a full **bitrate ladder**, and pre-positioning that content at the edge) before a single viewer ever presses play, which shifts the entire hard problem from upload-time processing to playback-time adaptation and placement.

### Problem Statement
Design a video-on-demand streaming service like Netflix: a fixed,
professionally produced catalog of movies and shows (not user uploads)
that subscribers stream on demand, with playback that stays smooth even
as their network conditions change mid-stream, and that works well
across a huge range of devices and countries. Design the system end to
end.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: Is content uploaded by users, or is it a curated catalog licensed/produced ahead of time?
*Why it matters:* A fixed, known catalog (thousands to tens of thousands of titles, not millions of uploads a day) changes everything: encoding can be done exhaustively and offline for every title, and content placement at edge nodes can be planned in advance rather than reacted to.

#### Q: Do viewers need the stream to adapt smoothly if their network conditions change mid-playback, like on a mobile network?
*Why it matters:* This decides whether we need true adaptive bitrate streaming (the player switching between pre-encoded quality levels seconds into a stream) versus just picking one bitrate at start time, which is a much simpler but worse experience.

#### Q: Should recommendations and personalization be in scope, or just catalog browsing and playback?
*Why it matters:* Recommendations are a large, separate ML system (built on watch history, collaborative filtering, ranking models) that could consume the entire interview on its own. Scoping it out keeps the focus on the streaming architecture itself.

#### Q: What's the expected concurrency, how many people are streaming simultaneously at peak, like a Friday evening?
*Why it matters:* Concurrent stream count, not catalog size, is what determines total sustained bandwidth needed, and that number is what justifies (or doesn't) building or leasing dedicated edge infrastructure versus using a generic third-party CDN.

### Functional Requirements
- A subscriber can browse a catalog of titles and select one to watch.
- A subscriber can start playback, and the stream quality adapts automatically as network conditions change, without the video stopping to buffer unnecessarily.
- A subscriber can resume a title from where they left off, on the same or a different device.
- The system supports multiple profiles per account, each with independent watch history.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- Playback must start quickly (sub-2-second startup is the bar) and must not stall or rebuffer noticeably under normal network variation.
- The system must sustain enormous simultaneous concurrent streaming load at peak hours (evenings, weekends) without degrading quality for any individual viewer.
- The system must serve a global audience with wildly different average network quality and last-mile ISP infrastructure per country/region.
- High availability for playback is non-negotiable: a subscriber paying for the service expects it to simply work every time they press play.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Peak concurrent bandwidth:** 50,000,000 concurrent streams * 3 Mbps ≈ 150 Tbps sustained at peak, which is the number that makes 'serve from a central datacenter' immediately implausible
- **Total encoded catalog size:** 15,000 titles * 1 hour avg * 5 GB/hour (full ladder) = 75 TB for the entire encoded catalog, which is small enough that it's plausible to cache most or all of it at every major edge location
- **Compute cost of encoding a title:** One-time cost per title, not per view: 10 rungs, each taking roughly real-time to a few times real-time to encode well; for a 1-hour title that's a bounded, poolable batch job, utterly different from a live per-upload cost model
- **Edge cache footprint needed to serve most requests locally:** 75 TB total catalog vs. modern edge storage nodes holding tens to low hundreds of TB each, meaning a well-provisioned edge node can hold the entire popular catalog locally, so the vast majority of playback requests never need to reach a distant origin at all

*Summary:* The number that shapes this whole design is that 75 TB (the entire encoded catalog) is **small enough to fit at the edge**, while 150 Tbps (peak concurrent playback bandwidth) is ==far too large to serve centrally==, so the winning move is to push nearly the whole catalog out to edge nodes ahead of time rather than fetching it on demand, which is the opposite instinct from a system with a catalog too large to pre-position.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
The source video is pre-encoded into independent rungs (e.g. 235p at 235 Kbps up through 4K at 16 Mbps), each cut into short segments (a few seconds each) that start and end at the same points across every rung. The client continuously measures its own recent download throughput and buffer health, and for each upcoming segment picks whichever rung best fits current conditions, requesting that segment from whichever rung it chose. Because segment boundaries line up across rungs, switching rungs between segments is seamless, no re-buffering, no restart.

#### undefined
A catalog this size (tens of terabytes) can fit almost entirely on edge storage appliances placed directly inside or very close to major ISP networks, an approach sometimes called an open, ISP-embedded edge model. Rather than paying a third-party CDN's transit and delivery costs at massive scale, boxes are shipped to and installed within ISP data centers, pre-loaded with the catalog (or the popular fraction of it) during off-peak hours, so the vast majority of streams never leave the ISP's own network.

lesson.content:
## Design a News Feed System (Facebook-style)

> **Core Concept:** The fan-out question a follow-graph feed already has to answer is secondary here; the real fight is where a personalized **ranking score** gets computed, at write time when it is cheap but cannot see the viewer or the ad inventory, or at read time when it is expensive but can score every candidate against the exact person looking and the exact ads available right now.

### Problem Statement
Design a news feed system like Facebook's: users have friends and follow
pages and groups, and the feed they see is not simple reverse-chronological
order, it is ranked, mixing organic content from friends, pages, and groups
with sponsored posts (ads), based on a relevance score computed for that
specific viewer. Design the system end to end.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: Is the feed pure reverse-chronological, or does it need to be ranked by relevance?
*Why it matters:* Chronological is the fan-out problem another case study already solves. Ranking adds an entirely separate scoring layer that has to run somewhere in the pipeline, and where it runs shapes the whole architecture.

#### Q: What signals does ranking use, and how fresh do they need to be? Likes and comments from minutes ago, or a model retrained daily?
*Why it matters:* If ranking needs signals from the last few minutes (a friend just commented on a post), the scoring step cannot be a stale, precomputed batch job, it has to touch something closer to real time.

#### Q: Do ads need to be mixed into the feed, and if so, do they need real-time auction logic (budget pacing, frequency capping) or can they be inserted at fixed positions?
*Why it matters:* Real-time ad auctions add a second ranking system that must be merged with organic ranking on the read path, which is a materially different and harder problem than simply reserving every fifth slot for an ad.

#### Q: How large is a typical candidate pool per feed request, meaning how many friends, pages, and groups does an average user follow?
*Why it matters:* If a user follows thousands of sources, scoring every single one of their recent posts with a heavy model on every feed load is computationally infeasible, which forces a multi-stage ranking funnel rather than a single scoring pass.

### Functional Requirements
- A user can post to their own timeline, visible to friends.
- A user can view a ranked home feed mixing posts from friends, followed pages, and joined groups.
- The feed must interleave sponsored posts (ads) among organic content according to some placement policy.
- User interactions (likes, comments, shares, hides) must feed back into future ranking as signals.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- Feed generation must complete quickly, well under a second, even though ranking is far more computationally expensive than pure chronological ordering.
- Ranking must incorporate near-real-time signals, a friend's comment from a minute ago should be able to influence what is shown right now, not tomorrow.
- Ad insertion must respect frequency caps and budget pacing without adding unacceptable latency to the read path.
- Ranking must degrade gracefully under system overload, falling back to a cheaper scoring method rather than failing the feed request entirely.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Feed requests per day:** 1,000,000,000 * 8 = 8 billion feed loads/day ≈ 92,593 requests/sec average, well above that at peak hours
- **Naive full-ranking scoring load:** 8,000,000,000 * 1,500 candidates = 12 trillion candidate scoring operations/day if every candidate got the expensive model on every request, this is the number that makes single-stage ranking impossible
- **After a cheap first-pass filter (1,500 -> 300 candidates):** 8,000,000,000 * 300 = 2.4 trillion heavy-model scoring operations/day ≈ 27.8 million/sec average, still enormous, requiring a large dedicated ranking service fleet
- **After a final shortlist for the expensive pass (300 -> 50 for final precise scoring):** 8,000,000,000 * 50 = 400 billion final-stage scoring operations/day ≈ 4.6 million/sec average, the volume the most accurate (and most expensive) model actually needs to handle

*Summary:* Scoring every candidate with a full ranking model on every feed load is computationally impossible at **12 trillion operations/day**, so the single fact that drives this architecture is that ranking has to be a **funnel**, cheap candidate generation and light filtering first, progressively narrowing the pool, with the most expensive and most accurate scoring reserved for only the last few hundred candidates.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
Write-time (precomputed) ranking would mean scoring a post for every potential viewer as soon as it is created and storing a per-viewer ordered feed, similar to a fan-out-on-write timeline cache. Read-time ranking means storing only a candidate pool at write time, and computing the actual relevance score fresh, for the specific viewer, at the moment they request their feed.

#### undefined
A highly accurate ranking model (deep learning based, using dozens of features per candidate) is expensive to run per item. Running it against a full candidate pool of roughly 1,500 items per feed load, across 8 billion feed loads a day, is not computationally feasible at any reasonable cost. The solution used at this scale is a multi-stage funnel: a very cheap heuristic or lightweight model narrows 1,500 candidates down to a few hundred, then a mid-cost model narrows further, and only the final, small shortlist gets the most expensive and most accurate model.

#### undefined
Organic ranking and ad ranking are computed by separate systems with different objectives: organic ranking optimizes for predicted engagement/relevance to the viewer, ad ranking optimizes for a combination of bid value, predicted engagement, and budget pacing for the advertiser. Both need to be reconciled into one ordered feed the user actually scrolls through.

## Design a Notification System

> **Core Concept:** This is a **fan-out plus retry** problem wearing a friendly UI: one internal event has to reliably reach the right user on the right channel, and reliably here means surviving a flaky provider ==without spamming the user twice==.

### Problem Statement
Design a notification system that can send a message to a user across
multiple channels (push notification, email, SMS), triggered by other
internal services (e.g. "order shipped", "someone liked your post").
Design the system end to end.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: Which channels need to be supported: push, email, SMS, in-app, or all of them?
*Why it matters:* Each channel has a different provider, different latency characteristics, and different failure modes; supporting all four multiplies the integration surface and the retry logic needed.

#### Q: Do users get to choose which channels they receive which notification types on?
*Why it matters:* Per-user, per-notification-type preferences mean a preference lookup has to sit in the pipeline before fan-out, not after, otherwise you send notifications you then have to apologize for.

#### Q: Do notifications need to be delivered in real time, or is a few seconds of delay acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Real-time delivery pushes toward a lean, low-latency path with minimal batching; a few seconds of slack allows batching multiple events together, which is cheaper and easier to make reliable.

#### Q: What's the expected volume, and are there bursty spikes (like a mass marketing campaign) on top of steady transactional traffic?
*Why it matters:* Steady one-at-a-time transactional notifications (an order shipped) and a marketing blast to 50 million users at once are very different load shapes that stress the queue and workers differently.

### Functional Requirements
- Accept a notification request from any internal service, specifying a user, a message, and a notification type.
- Deliver the notification via the user's preferred channel(s): push, email, or SMS.
- Respect user-level notification preferences (opted out of a given type or channel).
- Retry failed deliveries and record delivery status for observability.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- High availability: internal services calling this system should never be blocked or fail because the notification system is degraded.
- At-least-once delivery: a notification should never be silently dropped due to a transient provider failure.
- Must absorb bursty traffic (a marketing campaign to millions of users) without starving normal transactional notifications.
- Delivery latency for transactional notifications (order shipped) should typically be under a few seconds.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Steady-state notification QPS:** 50,000,000 * 1.3 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 750 deliveries/sec average, comfortably low
- **Campaign burst QPS:** 20,000,000 / 3,600 seconds ≈ 5,600 deliveries/sec sustained for that hour, roughly 7x normal steady load
- **Worker throughput needed:** If a single delivery worker can process ~50 sends/sec against a provider API, the campaign burst alone needs roughly 110-120 concurrent workers to keep pace

*Summary:* Steady traffic is small and easy, the entire capacity story is about surviving occasional large bursts, which is exactly what a queue between intake and delivery workers is for: it lets worker capacity scale to the burst without the intake API itself ever slowing down.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
If both a 'your order shipped' notification and a 20-million-user marketing blast go through the exact same queue with the same priority, the marketing blast can flood the queue and delay time-sensitive transactional notifications behind it. The fix is separating them into distinct queues (or priority tiers within one queue system) with independent worker pools, so a campaign's volume can never delay an order confirmation.

#### undefined
If a worker sends a push notification, then crashes before recording that it succeeded, a retry could resend the exact same notification, annoying the user. The fix is idempotency: each delivery attempt carries a unique idempotency key (derived from notification_id + channel), and either the provider itself supports deduplication by that key, or the worker checks and records delivery status atomically before considering a retry safe to send.

## Design a Parking Reservation System

> **Core Concept:** Most inventory systems treat availability as a single counter you decrement, but a parking spot isn't 'in stock' or 'out of stock,' it's booked for specific future time windows, so preventing a **double-booking** means checking whether two reservations' time windows **overlap**, not just checking whether a count is above zero.

### Problem Statement
Design a service like SpotHero: users search for parking spots near a
destination, reserve a specific spot for a specific future time window
(e.g. Saturday 6pm to 10pm), and pay for it, with the guarantee that a
reserved spot is actually available and physically theirs for that window.
Pricing can vary based on demand. Design the system end to end.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: Are reservations for a fixed future time window (e.g. 6pm-10pm), or is it walk-up/immediate parking with an unknown end time?
*Why it matters:* A fixed time window turns availability into an interval-overlap problem, checking whether a new reservation's window conflicts with any existing one for that spot. An open-ended walk-up model is simpler (a spot is just occupied or not, right now), but can't support the core product promise of booking in advance for a specific future time, which is the whole point of a reservation system.

#### Q: Can a single spot have back-to-back reservations with zero gap, or does the system need a buffer between bookings (for the previous driver to actually leave)?
*Why it matters:* Zero-gap booking maximizes utilization but risks a genuine physical conflict if the previous driver overstays even briefly. A mandatory buffer (say 15 minutes) trades a small amount of lost revenue per spot for a real-world safety margin against the single most common failure mode of this whole system: a spot that's reserved but still physically occupied.

#### Q: How does dynamic pricing work, is it a simple demand-based multiplier per lot, or does it need to vary by exact time slot and even by individual spot?
*Why it matters:* Per-lot demand pricing is a much simpler system: one price signal per lot, updated periodically. Per-slot, per-spot pricing is a genuinely more complex pricing engine that needs to price every remaining bookable interval independently, which materially changes both the data model and the read path for search results.

#### Q: What happens if a driver's reservation window ends and they haven't left, is that enforced automatically (e.g. via a connected gate/sensor), or is it purely a policy/fee issue handled after the fact?
*Why it matters:* Automatic enforcement (a physical gate, or a sensor confirming the spot is empty) makes the system's availability data trustworthy in real time. Without it, the system's 'available' state is a promise based on reservation records alone, and overstays silently erode the reliability of every subsequent booking for that spot, which the design needs to acknowledge and handle (e.g. via grace-period buffers and after-the-fact penalties) rather than pretend away.

### Functional Requirements
- A user can search for available parking spots near a destination for a specific date and time window.
- A user can reserve a specific available spot for a specific time window, and the reservation guarantees that spot is theirs for that window.
- The system prevents two reservations for the same spot from having overlapping time windows, even under concurrent booking attempts.
- Pricing for a given spot and time window can vary based on current demand for that lot and time.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- A reservation, once confirmed, must be a hard guarantee: no two confirmed reservations for the same spot may ever overlap in time, this is a correctness requirement, not best-effort.
- Search results (which spots are available for a given window) must reflect near-real-time availability; showing a spot as available that's actually already booked for that window creates a booking conflict at confirmation time.
- Booking confirmation should complete within a couple of seconds, since a user comparing multiple lots will abandon a slow checkout.
- The system should handle popular events (a stadium concert) driving a burst of concurrent search and booking traffic for the same small set of lots without booking failures or overselling.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Bookings per second, average:** 200,000 / 86,400 sec ≈ 2.3 bookings/sec average, far higher at peak (event nights, weekday morning commute)
- **Searches per second, average:** 2.3 bookings/sec * 15 (search-to-book ratio) ≈ 35 searches/sec average
- **Overlap checks per search:** 35 searches/sec * 20 lots ≈ 700 lot-level availability checks/sec, each a bounded interval-overlap query against that lot's existing reservations, not a full-table scan
- **Reservations per spot per day:** 200,000 reservations / 500,000 spots ≈ 0.4 reservations per spot per day on average, confirming most of the system's spots are lightly booked most of the time, with real load concentrated in a minority of popular lots

*Summary:* The driving fact is that this system is comfortably low-volume in raw throughput (a few bookings per second on average) but has a strict correctness requirement under concurrency, so the design challenge isn't scale, it's guaranteeing that a burst of near-simultaneous booking attempts for the same popular spot and time window (a stadium event) can never both succeed.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
A typical e-commerce inventory system tracks 'N units in stock' and decrements on purchase, a single number. A parking spot doesn't have a single availability state, it can be free from 6am-2pm and booked from 2pm-6pm on the same day, so 'is this spot available' is really 'is this spot available for this specific requested window,' which means checking the new reservation's [start_time, end_time) against every existing reservation for that spot for any overlap, not decrementing a count. This is the same class of problem as calendar/meeting-room booking systems.

#### undefined
Two users can both view a spot as available and both submit a booking request within the same second, especially for a popular spot near a stadium right before an event. If the overlap check and the insert are two separate operations (read existing reservations, decide there's no conflict, then write), a race window exists where both requests pass the check before either writes, and both succeed, producing a genuine double-booking. This has to be closed with either a database-level constraint that makes overlapping rows for the same spot physically impossible to insert, or an explicit transaction with strong enough isolation that the check-then-insert sequence is atomic.

#### undefined
Computing a live demand price on every search request (based on real-time booking velocity for that lot and time slot) adds computation cost to the hottest, most latency-sensitive path in the system. Instead, a background job periodically (e.g. every few minutes, or triggered by booking-velocity thresholds) recomputes a demand multiplier per lot per time slot and writes it to a fast-to-read snapshot, which both search and booking simply read rather than compute.
